messages.content: Repair one STORY-001 section without changing its scene boundary. Remove the listed forbidden generic/lore concepts and replace any explanatory machine internals with directly observable sound, motion, heat, objects and consequences. Return first-person story prose only; do not add new proper nouns or backstory.

PART 04/08 — The line remembers wrongly. Aim for 345-430 words.
Forbidden concepts present: reactor core, optical sensor, logic gate.

SECTION-SPECIFIC REPAIR:
Show the sorting/production line behaving wrongly only through visible movement, sound, objects and consequences. Remove optical-sensor, reactor-core, data-system and mind-reading explanations. Keep spatial causality clear and end with the companion on the dangerous side.

GLOBAL CONTRACT:
First-person Sprocket memory; tactile and mechanically uncertain. Keep the incident linear: trigger -> boundary -> hatch -> wrong line -> failed rescue -> scrap intervention -> tradeoff/line-stop -> escape/missing-noise frame. No new proper nouns, institutions, grand backstory, holograms, data streams, reactors, destiny language or generic cyberpunk decoration. Never repeat a sentence or paragraph. Do not explain the machine's internal logic. The companion remains unnamed and their final fate may remain genuinely unresolved, but never state both alive and dead. Return only story prose with 3-6 paragraphs.

CURRENT RENDER:
The smell hit me first, thick and wrong, like burnt copper and wet wool. It wasn't the clean ozone of a standard fault; this was the scent of something organic being ground into the metal. The hum started as a vibration in the floorboards, a low thrum that traveled up through my soles and settled in my teeth. I stood before the sorting gantry, my fingers tracing the cold, oily rail where the conveyor belt's teeth should have been. It wasn't just moving; it was grinding. The machinery had a rhythm, a desperate, stuttering cadence that spoke of a loop running too long, too hot.

I watched the optical sensors flicker, their red eyes scanning the incoming stream of scrap metal and auto-parts. The line remembers wrongly. That was the phrase that kept looping in my head, a glitch in the logic gate. The system was classifying a specific batch of corroded reactor cores as standard insulation, routing them straight into the secondary melting chamber. But those cores weren't insulation; they were the very fuel that powered the district's grid. If they hit the melt, the pressure would spike, the containment would fail, and the whole block would go dark.

A heavy, rusted casing slid onto the belt, its surface pitted and dark. The sensor arm swiveled, a mechanical eye blinking red, then green, then red again. It was a cycle of error, a repeated mistake that the machine had learned to ignore. The gears were turning with a sound like grinding stones, the metal screeching against the belt. I could see the spark, a tiny, dangerous arc jumping between the sensor and the core's casing. The line was misidentifying the hazard, treating a ticking time bomb as harmless debris.

My companion was waiting near the intake chute, their hands hovering over the emergency override, but they were too far away to reach the critical junction. The machine's logic was flawed, a blind spot in its vision. It saw the shape, not the function. It saw the metal, not the danger. The conveyor belt moved forward, relentless and indifferent, carrying the misclassified core toward the heart of the furnace.

I had to act. The line remembered wrongly, and I was the only one who could make it right. I stepped forward, my boots clicking on the grating, the smell of ozone and burnt oil filling the air. The gears were turning faster now, the vibration intensifying. The machine was about to process the error, to turn the mistake into a catastrophe. I had to break the loop, to stop the hum, before the line's memory of the wrong path became permanent. The stakes were high, the danger real, and the only way to save my companion was to force the machine to see the truth, to make it understand that some things could not be sorted, only stopped. I reached for the manual cut-off, my hand slipping on the slick grating as the belt roared closer, the heat radiating against my skin, the line stopping just inches from my grasp, the companion still standing on the wrong side of the moving metal.
